description: Collision theory, factors affecting reaction rate, and practical methods for measuring rate.
content_html:
What Is Rate of Reaction?

The rate of reaction tells us how quickly a reaction happens. A fast reaction, such as an explosion, is over in a fraction of a second. A slow reaction, such as the rusting of iron or the weathering of stone, takes months or years. In industry, controlling the rate of a reaction is vital — too fast can be dangerous, too slow is uneconomical.

Rate can be measured in several ways: the volume of gas produced per unit time (using a gas syringe or measuring cylinder over water), the mass of a reaction mixture lost per unit time (as gas escapes, measured using a balance), or the time taken for a colour change or for a solution to become opaque. The choice depends on the particular reaction and what can be conveniently measured.

Collision Theory

Collision theory states that for a reaction to occur, the reacting particles must: (1) collide with each other, (2) collide with sufficient energy (at least the activation energy), and (3) collide with the correct orientation. Not every collision leads to a reaction — most are unsuccessful because the particles bounce off without reacting. The rate of reaction depends on the frequency of successful collisions: collisions that have both enough energy and the right orientation.

Key Fact

For a reaction to happen, particles must collide with enough energy (the activation energy) and the correct orientation. Anything that increases the frequency or energy of successful collisions increases the rate of reaction.

Factors Affecting Rate of Reaction

Four main factors affect the rate of a chemical reaction: temperature, concentration, surface area, and catalysts.

Temperature: Increasing the temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, so they move faster and collide more frequently. More importantly, a greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or exceeding the activation energy, so a much larger fraction of collisions are successful. Even a small increase in temperature produces a significant increase in rate.

Concentration (for solutions) and pressure (for gases): Increasing concentration means more particles in the same volume, so they collide more frequently. For gases, increasing pressure pushes particles closer together, with the same effect. More collisions per unit time → more successful collisions → faster rate.

Surface area: Breaking a solid into smaller pieces increases the surface area to volume ratio. A greater surface area means more of the solid is exposed to the other reactant, so collisions occur more frequently. Powdered marble chips react faster with hydrochloric acid than large lumps, even with the same total mass. In extreme cases, a fine powder of combustible material in air can cause a dust explosion.

Catalysts

A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction without being used up. It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful. On a reaction profile, the catalyst lowers the peak (activation energy) without changing the energy levels of the reactants or products. Each catalyst is specific to a particular reaction — iron catalyses the Haber process but would not catalyse the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide (which uses manganese dioxide).

Key Fact

Catalysts speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy. They are not used up and are not changed at the end of the reaction. Enzymes are biological catalysts found in all living organisms.

Interpreting Rate of Reaction Graphs

Rate graphs typically plot volume of gas (or mass lost) on the y-axis against time on the x-axis. The gradient (steepness) of the line at any point shows the rate at that moment — a steeper gradient means a faster rate. The line levels off when one reactant is used up (the reaction is complete). Two curves on the same axes that level off at the same point but with different steepnesses represent the same reaction with the same amount of reactant, but at different rates (e.g. different temperatures or concentrations).

In your practical work (PAG C5), you investigate the rate of reaction between a metal (such as magnesium) and dilute acid, or between marble chips and hydrochloric acid. Methods include:

  • Gas syringe: collect gas in a syringe and record volume at regular intervals.
  • Displacement of water: collect gas over water in an inverted measuring cylinder.
  • Mass loss: place the flask on a balance; record mass at regular intervals as gas escapes through cotton wool.
  • Disappearing cross: for the sodium thiosulfate and acid reaction, time how long it takes for a cross viewed through the solution to disappear as a precipitate of sulfur forms.

In all methods, change only one variable at a time and keep all other conditions constant to make it a fair test. Look for anomalous results in your data and exclude them when calculating means.
exam_tip_html: For 3-mark Explain questions about factors affecting rate, always give a three-step answer: (1) state what changes (e.g. temperature increases), (2) link to collision theory (e.g. particles have more kinetic energy, collide more frequently and with more energy), (3) give the consequence for rate (e.g. more successful collisions per second, so rate increases). Generic responses like ‘particles collide more’ without explaining why collisions increase will only score 1 or 2 marks. A common mistake is saying catalysts are ‘used up’ — they are not, and stating this will lose marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Rate of reaction measures how quickly reactants are used up or products are formed. Collision theory: particles must collide with enough energy (activation energy) and correct orientation for a reaction to occur.
  • Increasing temperature, concentration (or pressure for gases) and surface area all increase the rate by increasing the frequency and/or energy of successful collisions. Catalysts lower the activation energy by providing an alternative pathway — they are not used up.
  • Rate graphs: steeper gradient = faster rate; the line levels off when a reactant is used up. PAG C5 involves measuring rate by gas collection (syringe or displacement) or mass loss. Change only one variable at a time for a fair test.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following explains why increasing temperature increases the rate of reaction?
A) Particles become smaller so they can collide more easily
B) Particles have more energy, so more collisions have sufficient energy to react
C) The activation energy decreases as temperature increases
D) Particles dissolve more readily at higher temperatures
practice_questions.marks: B) Particles have more energy, so more collisions have sufficient energy to react [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which you could increase the rate of a reaction between marble chips (calcium carbonate) and hydrochloric acid.
practice_questions.marks: Any two of: increase temperature; increase concentration of acid; crush/grind the marble chips into a powder (increase surface area); add a catalyst. [1 mark for any two correct]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a gas syringe can be used to measure the rate of the reaction between magnesium ribbon and dilute hydrochloric acid.
practice_questions.marks: Collect hydrogen gas produced in a gas syringe connected to the reaction flask [1 mark]; record the volume of gas at regular time intervals (e.g. every 30 seconds) and plot volume against time [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain how increasing the concentration of hydrochloric acid increases the rate of its reaction with magnesium ribbon, using ideas from collision theory.
practice_questions.marks: Increasing concentration means there are more acid particles (H⁺ ions) in the same volume [1 mark]; the frequency of collisions between H⁺ ions and magnesium particles increases [1 mark]; so more successful collisions occur per unit time and the rate increases [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
A student investigates how the surface area of marble chips affects the rate of reaction with dilute hydrochloric acid. She uses the same mass of marble in each experiment but varies the size of the chips.

(a) Identify the independent variable, dependent variable, and one control variable in this investigation. [3 marks]
(b) The student collects the gas using a gas syringe and records the volume every 30 seconds. Sketch the shape of the graph she would expect if small chips react faster than large chips, but the same total volume of gas is produced in both experiments. [1 mark]
practice_questions.marks: (a) Independent: size/surface area of marble chips [1 mark]; dependent: volume of gas produced / rate of reaction [1 mark]; control: mass of marble, volume/concentration of acid, temperature [1 mark — any one]; (b) Two curves levelling off at the same point: the small chips curve is steeper initially (faster rate) but both curves level off at the same final volume of gas [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction. In your answer, include:
• what a catalyst does to the activation energy
• how this is shown on a reaction profile
• what happens to the catalyst at the end of the reaction
• why different reactions require different catalysts.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy [1 mark]; on the reaction profile this is shown as a lower peak / smaller hump, while reactant and product energy levels are unchanged [1 mark]; a greater proportion of collisions now have sufficient energy to react, increasing the rate [1 mark]; catalyst is not used up / not permanently changed at the end [1 mark]; catalysts are specific because the alternative pathway depends on the interaction between the catalyst's active site/surface and particular reactant molecules [1 mark]; overall energy change of the reaction is not affected by the catalyst [1 mark].
Secure: Most of the above correctly stated; reaction profile correctly described; catalyst specificity noted.
Developing: Activation energy lowered and catalyst not used up both stated; profile or specificity partially addressed.
Emerging: Basic statement that catalyst speeds up reactions; limited mechanistic explanation.

knowledge_checks.q: What does a catalyst do to the activation energy of a reaction?
A rate-of-reaction graph levels off. What does this indicate?
options: One of the reactants has been used up

knowledge_checks.q: Collision theory states that particles must collide with sufficient _____ and the correct orientation for a reaction to occur.
Crushing marble chips into a powder increases the _____ to volume ratio, which increases the rate of reaction with acid.
Match each factor to its effect on collision frequency:
right: Particles move faster and collide more often with more energy
More particles in the same volume, more frequent collisions
Provides a lower energy pathway, more successful collisions

flashcard_questions.q: What is the rate of reaction?
flashcard_questions.a: A measure of how quickly reactants are used up or products are formed.

flashcard_questions.q: State the three conditions required for a successful collision according to collision theory.
flashcard_questions.a: Particles must collide, with sufficient energy (activation energy), and the correct orientation.

flashcard_questions.q: How does increasing temperature affect the rate of reaction?
flashcard_questions.a: Particles gain more kinetic energy, collide more often and with more energy, so more collisions are successful.

flashcard_questions.q: How does increasing concentration affect the rate of reaction?
flashcard_questions.a: More particles in the same volume means collisions happen more frequently.

flashcard_questions.q: How does increasing surface area affect the rate of reaction?
flashcard_questions.a: More of the solid is exposed, so collisions between reactant particles happen more frequently.
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, without being used up.
Biological catalysts (proteins) that speed up reactions in living organisms.

flashcard_questions.q: Does a catalyst change the energy levels of reactants or products?
flashcard_questions.a: No — it only lowers the activation energy (the peak on the reaction profile).

flashcard_questions.q: On a rate-of-reaction graph, what does a steeper gradient indicate?
Why do two rate curves on the same graph that level off at the same point indicate the same amount of reactant?
flashcard_questions.a: The same amount of product is formed, so the same amount of reactant was used up.

flashcard_questions.q: What PAG practical involves investigating the rate of reaction between marble chips and hydrochloric acid?
flashcard_questions.a: PAG C5 — rates of reaction investigation.

glossary_terms.definition: A measure of how quickly reactants are used up or products are formed in a chemical reaction.
The theory that reactions can only occur when particles collide with sufficient energy and the correct orientation.
The ratio of exposed surface to the volume of a solid, which increases when the solid is broken into smaller pieces.
A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction by providing an alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy, without being used up itself.
Biological catalysts (proteins) that speed up reactions in living organisms by providing a specific active site.
The minimum energy that reacting particles must have in order to collide successfully and react.
